examples.question_text:
(a) A rectangular box is $7$ cm long, $5$ cm wide and $3$ cm high. Find its volume.
(b) A rectangular storeroom is $9$ m long, $5$ m wide and $4$ m high. Find its volume.
examples.solution_text:
(a) One layer contains $7\times5=35$ cubic-centimetre units.
$35\times3=105$.
The volume is $105\text{ cm}^3$.
(b) $9\times5=45$ cubic-metre units in one layer.
$45\times4=180$.
The volume is $180\text{ m}^3$.

examples.question_text: A cube has edges of $7$ cm. A student writes $7\times7=49\text{ cm}^2$ as its volume. Explain and correct the error.
examples.solution_text:
$7\times7=49$ gives the number of cubic-centimetre units in one layer. There are $7$ layers.
$49\times7=343$.
The student left out the height and recorded area units. The volume is $343\text{ cm}^3$.

examples.question_text: A rectangular box has dimensions $80$ mm, $7$ cm and $3$ cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
examples.solution_text:
Use centimetres for every dimension.
$80\text{ mm}=8\text{ cm}$.
$8\times7=56$.
$56\times3=168$.
The volume is $168\text{ cm}^3$.

examples.question_text: A rectangular prism has volume $390\text{ cm}^3$. Its length is $13$ cm and its width is $5$ cm. Find its height and check the answer.
examples.solution_text:
$13\times5=65$ cubic-centimetre units in one layer.
$390\div65=6$ layers.
The height is $6$ cm.
Check: $13\times5\times6=390\text{ cm}^3$.

Find the number of cubic-centimetre units in one layer, then multiply by the number of layers.
$\begin{align*}8.5\times4&=34\\34\times2&=68\end{align*}$
The volume is $68\text{ cm}^3$.

methods.description: Multiply length by width to find the number of unit cubes in one layer, then multiply by height. Use cubic centimetres or cubic metres, including decimal dimensions where assessed.

coverage.summary: Retained all four existing examples exactly and added one editable, unshaded rectangular-prism diagram example with a decimal dimension. All three distinct assessed methods are covered; assessment fields were read only for classification and were neither changed nor re-audited. New working gives 34 units per layer and 68 cubic centimetres in total. Its diagram has explicit face topology, view-derived hidden edges, black non-drawing dimension labels authored at 10 pt, and no answer annotations in the question. Solutions rely on the implemented blue renderer styling. Actual capture, final-size label verification and independent review of the new example remain later stages.

examples.derivation: Independently calculated 8.5 × 4 = 34 cubic-centimetre units per layer, then 34 × 2 = 68 cm³. This adapts the rectangular-prism task in source image53 and uses the layer method taught at lines 124–142. Decimal dimensions are already assessed. The diagram labels agree with the calculation.

review.summary: All 22 exact assessment locators map to the three covered methods: rectangular-prism layers, cube volume and missing dimension. The four retained examples match the baseline exactly and have no genuine gutter, diagram or annotation defects. The supplementary conversion example is retained under the explicit instruction. Example 4 is source-aligned, mathematically correct and within scope. Its aligned equations have independent left-hand sides, so no phantom equals is required. Solution prose and mathematics inherit the implemented blue styling. Final-size typography and visual capture remain for the later rendering stage. Accepted assessment mathematics was not re-audited.
